analysis.one_liner: Treats guns and ammunition like other consumer products, letting the government set safety standards and order recalls.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in March 1999 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress adjourned in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given the Treasury Secretary authority, similar to what the Consumer Product Safety Commission has over other products, to regulate the design, manufacture, and sale of firearms, firearm parts, ammunition, and BB guns. It would allow safety regulations, recalls, repairs, refunds, factory and record inspections, fines of $5,000 to $10,000 per violation, private lawsuits, and up to two years in prison for knowing repeat violations. It also would have created a government clearinghouse for data on gun deaths and injuries. It never received any committee action or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers and families: firearms, ammunition, and even BB guns would have been subject to federal safety testing, labeling, and recall requirements, and victims could sue for damages when a defective product injured them. The public would also gain access to government research on gun injuries and deaths.

how_it_helps.text: It would have required the Treasury Secretary to write safety regulations governing the design, manufacture, and performance of firearms, firearm parts, ammunition, and BB guns, aimed at preventing 'unreasonable risk of injury.'

The Secretary could order the recall, repair, or replacement of a defective firearm product, require refunds, and outright ban manufacture of a product found to pose an unreasonable risk to the public.

It would have created a Firearm Injury Information Clearinghouse and required annual public reporting on firearm deaths, injuries, and industry compliance — data that would help consumers compare the safety of products.
Victims and any interested person could sue violators in federal court for damages and attorney's fees, and could even sue to enforce the Act directly.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and pawnbrokers, who would face testing, certification, labeling, recordkeeping, and inspection requirements, fines per violation, and private lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have given the Treasury Secretary broad authority to restrict the manufacture and sale of any firearm product found to pose an 'unreasonable risk,' including a ban on products whose availability the Secretary judged excessive — a power critics viewed as gun control by regulation rather than pure product safety oversight.

Manufacturers and dealers would bear new compliance costs: testing and certifying every product, labeling, detailed recordkeeping open to federal inspection, and potential fines of $5,000 per product per violation, rising to $10,000 — penalties that would fall hardest on small dealers.
The bill also authorized private lawsuits against manufacturers and dealers for damages and enforcement, increasing litigation exposure beyond the government's own actions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were potentially large: a permanent safety regulator for firearms could have prevented deaths and injuries from defective or unsafe guns, just as similar agencies did for cars and toys, and would have given buyers real safety information [S2][S3]. The costs were real but narrower: compliance and recordkeeping costs for manufacturers and dealers, and — the strongest good-faith objection — a permanent authority over how guns are designed, which opponents feared could be used to restrict firearms availability beyond fixing product defects [S3]. The bill was never seriously weighed in committee; the record shows no hearing, no markup, and no vote [S5], so the country got neither the safety protections nor any tested evidence of the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it expired quietly at the end of the 106th Congress in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Torricelli introduced S. 534 on March 4, 1999, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
That referral is the last recorded action; the bill received no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

The bill would have extended to firearms the kind of consumer product safety regulation that applies to products like cars and toys, including recall orders, inspections, fines, and a public research clearinghouse.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The firearms industry, which kept the consumer product safety exemption in place.

for.name: Sen. Robert Torricelli
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed proposals to give federal agencies consumer-product-style authority over firearms and pressed the Senate not to act on them.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats; the bill died in committee without a recorded vote, so no bipartisan coalition ever formed around it.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed mandatory safety testing, labeling, certification, recordkeeping, factory inspections, and recall authority on gun makers, ending the industry's status as a consumer product exempt from federal safety regulation [S3].
Dealers and pawnbrokers would face labeling duties, inspection of their records, fines per defective product sold, and private lawsuits, with penalties of $5,000 to $10,000 per violation [S3].

The bill would have institutionalized federal collection of production and sales figures for every licensed manufacturer, folding the industry permanently into a federal oversight regime similar to other consumer product industries [S2][S3].
